Q: How to handle option-drag in iOS version of multi-platform app? A:

UIEvent has a modifier flags property as you say, but on macOS there is a static method NSEvent.modifierFlags that gives you the state of the keyboard modifiers at any point.

On iOS you can only get modifierFlags in a keyboard event, and I don't know of a way to interrogate the modifier keys during the handling of a touch event (Like I can in the .onChanged handler of my DragGesture on macOS.

Q: Sending data to Thymeleaf (HTML) from Spring-Boot MVC (Java), Not being displayed A:

You should probably use return "index"; in the controller.

And if span is not working for you you can try blocks:

<th:block th:text="${name}"></th:block>

Which you can use in h3 too.

Q: Global Gradle proxy settings A:

Yes, it seems possible. See here, especially:

We can define a gradle.properties file and set the property in this file. We can place the file in our project directory or in the <USER_HOME>/.gradle directory. The properties defined in the property file in our home directory take precedence over the properties defined in the file in our project directory. As a bonus we can also define system properties in a gradle.properties file, we only have to prefix the property name with systemProp..

The gradle.properties files can be found at the following paths:

# Windows Gradle file
%userprofile%\.gradle\gradle.properties

# Linux Gradle file
~/.gradle/gradle.properties

Q: I am getting an error when Importing csv file into PostgreSQL A:

Sometimes CSV import errors occur due to encoding mismatch.

In my case, the file was not actually UTF-8 encoded (although UTF-8 is common), but closer to LATIN1. This caused errors during import in PostgreSQL. After selecting the correct encoding, the data imported successfully.

Steps to import using pgAdmin4:

  1. Navigate to: Database → Schemas → public → Tables → right-click your table → Import/Export Data

  2. General Tab:

    • Select Import
    • Choose your CSV file
    • Format: CSV
    • Encoding: Try UTF-8 first; if it fails, use LATIN1 or WIN1252

  3. Options Tab:

    • Header: ON (if your CSV has column names)
    • Delimiter: ,
    • Quote: "(check what your file use single or double quote)
    • Escape: "(check what your file use single or double quote)

  4. Click OK to import the data

Q: Make this code shorter and more optimized? DL 3155E24 || I/0 03 A:

I just had a good idea for generating the bitmaps instead of looking them up: shift another one-hot bitmap to the right starting from 80h, and OR them. (Or in this case, add them works too since they don't overlap).

My earlier suggestions (lodsb and using shl bl,1 / jnz as the inner loop condition) get your version down from 45 bytes to 38 bytes (saving 7). My bit-shift idea saves another 5 bytes, down 33 bytes. Would be nice to somehow golf another 1 byte off of this so it would fit in 2 paragraphs, needing no padding for the next chunk of code to start at a 16-byte aligned segment boundary.

I tested this under Linux (built as a 32-bit static executable) with GDB to verify that AL takes values 81h / 42h / 24h / 18h, 18h, 24h, 42h, 81h. (I replaced the out / int instructions with nop, and set a breakpoint after the lea so I could hit c (continue) repeatedly and look at EAX in layout reg TUI mode.) nasm -f elf prog-bitshift-lea.asm / ld -melf_i386 prog-bitshift-lea.o to make a static executable with this code as the ELF entry point at the start of the .text section.

I checked code size by building it as a 16-bit flat binary, of course; instruction lengths are different in 32-bit mode although interestingly this version is the same total length with 2-byte out/int replaced by 1-byte nop. nasm -l /dev/stdout prog-bitshift-lea.asm to make a listing to stdout.

org 0

PROGR:
    MOV AL, 89H
    OUT 13H,AL

CICLO:
    MOV BL, 01H    ; 2-byte instruction
    MOV SI, 80h    ; 3-byte instruction
NEXT:
    xor ax, ax
    OUT 10h, AL
    lea ax, [bx+si]  ; adding is equivalent to ORing since the bitmaps don't intersect
    OUT 11h, AL
    MOV AL,  BL
    OUT 10h, AL
    MOV AL, 1   ; producing AX=1 due to AX upper half being 0.
    INT 1CH

    shr si, 1   ; TODO schedule this after an OUT for better prefetch buffer usage
    SHL BL, 1
    JNZ NEXT
; inner loop size: 16 bytes

    JMP CICLO

; size: db $-$$   ; current position - start of segment = 0x21 = 33 bytes of code before this.

LEA costs 2+EA cycles on 8088. The effective-address calculation time for [bx+si] is 7 cycles, so only 9 cycles total for that instruction, and 11 for lea + shr reg,1, faster than lodsb (16 cycles) which in turn is faster than mov al, [si] (12+5c) / inc si (3c). (https://www2.math.uni-wuppertal.de/~fpf/Uebungen/GdR-SS02/opcode_i.html). But that's ignoring the code-fetch bottleneck, which is usually dominant on 8088 (8-bit bus), and sometimes on 8086 (16-bit bus). Maybe even here with so many out instructions.

Inner loop size isn't as compact, so more cycles will be spent on code-fetch in it, but less time on data fetch. (An additional 3 bytes of code = 12 cycles, on 8088, unless there's idle time for the prefetch buffer. But only 8 cycles difference when we account for not doing a data load.) 8086 fetches 2 bytes at a time into a 6-byte buffer, 8088 1 byte at a time into a 4-byte buffer.

int is a branch that sends execution elsewhere, so prefetch past it is wasted. Before it would be a good place to schedule some of the loop overhead like the shr si,1, since that's a fast 2-byte instruction that along with mov al,1 will leave the prefetch buffer empty on 8088 ahead of the int, and close to empty on 8086.

Unless the int handler is extremely tiny, that'll probably be a significant fraction of the total execution time.

For comparison, I got the lookup table version down to 38 bytes:

%use MASM    ;; NASM compat package for MASM syntax like "offset"
org 0
PROGR:
    MOV AL, 89H
    OUT 13H,AL
    ; cld  ; if we can't assume DF=0

CICLO:
    MOV BL, 01H
    MOV SI, offset BITMAPS ; below
NEXT:
    xor AX,  AX
    OUT 10h, AL
    ;MOV AL, [SI]
    ;INC SI
    lodsb
    OUT 11h, AL
    MOV AL,  BL
    OUT 10h, AL
    MOV AL, 1   ; producing AX=1 due to AX=0 earlier.
    INT 1CH

    SHL BL,1
    JNZ NEXT
; inner loop size = 13 bytes

    JMP CICLO

BITMAPS:          ; still in the code segment, so assuming DS=CS
    DB 81H, 42H, 24H, 18H, 18H, 24H, 42H, 81H

; size: db $-$$   ; 0x26 = 38 bytes of code+data

Both are a huge improvement over the OP's original 159 bytes fully unrolled loop, of course.

Q: Refused to frame 'https://sis-t.redsys.es:25443/' because an ancestor violates the following Content Security Policy: "frame-ancestors 'none'" A:

You MUST contact Redsys Support and ask them to add your domain / subdomain in the "list of accepted domains for InSite". Once they have added it in, it will show up in the Admin page under Administracion (icono maletin) > Comercio > Datos de Configuracion > Dominios InSite Permitidos.

You can probably not enable this yourself, so you need support to do this for you.

Once you leave the Testing Environment and move to the Real Environment, you will need to add the domains again.
